newsitem.title: USA: Albright gets sympathetic House hearing on budget.
newsitem.headline: Albright gets sympathetic House hearing on budget.

text.p: Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, in her debut before Congress in her new job, won a sympathetic reception on Tuesday as she called for a rise in the State Department's budget after a decade of declines.

Albright, defending a request for a budget increase of nearly seven per cent to $19.45 billion, told the House of Representatives International Relations Committee that under current trends "diplomatically, we are steadily and unilaterally disarming ourselves".
"Diplomatic readiness is not a luxury, it is an imperative," she declared. "We cannot have world-class diplomacy on the cheap".

Committee chairman Benjamin Gilman, a New York Republican, told Albright that Congress was ready to work with her on the 1998 budget in the spirit of bipartisanship that Democratic President Bill Clinton has proclaimed for his second term.

Gilman said the budget request, plus a $3.5 billion "agreement to borrow" for the International Monetary Fund and a $921 million arrears payment for the United Nations, was "a tall order." But he said the plans were negotiatiable.

"Madame Secretary, we look forward to working with you to produce an authorisation bill that provides for a reasonable plan for payment of our U.N. arrears, for State Department operations and for some foreign assistance," he said.

Albright noted that over the last four years, the State Department had cut more than 2,000 employees and closed more than 30 foreign posts. She recounted visiting some U.S. embassies where ambassadors washed dishes in bathtubs.

"Our spending on international affairs constitutes barely one percent of the federal budget. If this small amount were to be cut further, it is our influence in the world, not the (U.S. budget) deficit, that would decline," she said.
Many of the same arguments were made by former Secretary of State Warren Christopher, but his low-key style failed to sway Congress or arrest the decline in foreign spending.
Albright, by contrast, appeared determined to use her charisma and force of personality to get her way, and many members of the committee seemed overawed.

She began the hearing with a joke about the name-plate in front of her, which identified her as Ambassador rather than Secretary Albright, a hang-over from her former job as U.N. envoy. "Do you all know something I don't?" she asked.

Albright won an instant compliment from Lee Hamilton of Indiana, the top Democrat on the committee. "These past few days have been difficult for you in many ways, yet you are off to a remarkable start as secretary of state," he said.
Hamilton was apparently referring to disclosures that Albright's grandparents were Jews who died in the Holocaust. The Czech-born Albright was brought up as a Roman Catholic.
Hamilton said he personally would support an increase in foreign spending, but added: "It's not going to be easy."

Albright spoke out vigorously for paying off more than $1 billion in arrears to the United Nations, despite the deep unpopularity of the world body in Congress, which believes it squanders funds and frustrates U.S. policies.

Under the Clinton administration's plan, Congress would appropriate the funds now, but they would only be paid in 1999 if Washington and the United Nations can agree on cutting the U.S. share of the U.N. budget.
"Our continued leadership at the U.N. depends upon it. Our principles require it. Our budget allows it. And our interests demand it," Albright said.
Gilman said Congress would need "real U.N. reform" if it was to approve the plan, but he did not appear to rule it out.
